recipes.title: Rosemary pecan brittle
recipes.subtitle: With mature cheddar
batch: **Batch** Half the published brittle recipe. **Estimated usable yield is about 25–30 small canapé shards**, working at roughly **10–12 g brittle per shard** and allowing for pan residue and awkward fragments. This is a planning estimate, not a tested yield. The sugar, nuts and butter total **369 g before cooking** (198 + 114 + 57 g); finished weight and intact shard count remain unmeasured. Eight guests are confirmed; the served count per guest remains open. Suggested assembly is one thin, bite-sized shard with **10 g mature cheddar**, a working portion rather than an agreed allocation. Reserve surplus brittle separately.

items: Set out scales, teaspoon measures, a heavy saucepan, wooden spoon, candy thermometer, heatproof spatula and oven gloves. Use a pan that allows the thermometer probe to sit in the caramel without touching its base.
Line a large rimmed baking tray with baking parchment or a silicone mat. Have a separate ovenproof dish for the nuts and an airtight container for the cooled brittle.

Chop **114 g pecans** into small pieces. Cut **57 g room-temperature unsalted butter** into pieces. Measure **198 g granulated sugar**. Divide both **1½ tsp finely chopped fresh rosemary** and **1½ tsp flaky sea salt** into two **¾ tsp portions**. Set out **¼ tsp maple extract**, if using.

Keep the cheddar separate, refrigerated according to its label. Have a board and knife ready for finishing. Prepare this brittle separately from the pistachio dessert shards, even if making both in one session.

rows.amount: 57 g, room temperature, cut into pieces

rows.name: Fresh rosemary
rows.amount: 1½ tsp finely chopped leaves, divided into ¾ tsp in the caramel and ¾ tsp on top

rows.name: Flaky sea salt
rows.amount: 1½ tsp, divided into ¾ tsp in the caramel and ¾ tsp on top

rows.name: Maple extract
rows.amount: ¼ tsp, proposed subtle starting amount

rows.amount: Suggested 10 g per served shard; total TBD once count is agreed

notes: Use large flaky salt, not the same spoonful of fine salt. Flake size affects saltiness. Maple is optional; keep the sugar quantity intact and use extract rather than substituting syrup.

steps.title: Warm the equipment and nuts
steps.text: Heat the oven to **95°C conventional**. Warm the lined tray and **114 g chopped pecans** separately while preparing the caramel. The nuts should be warm when added, not browned.
steps.aside: This warming cue is our adaptation of the source's slightly warmed nuts.

steps.title: Caramelise
steps.text: Heat **198 g sugar** in the saucepan, stirring until melted, then stop stirring. Start on high heat, reducing to medium-high as it melts; lower further if colouring unevenly. Cook to medium amber, going by colour rather than temperature.

steps.title: Finish cooking
steps.text: Stir in **114 g warm pecans**, then **57 g butter**. Stir until incorporated and the mixture reaches **149°C (300°F)**. It takes about two minutes; use the endpoint, not the clock.

steps.title: Season and spread
steps.text: Remove from the heat. Stir in **¾ tsp rosemary**, **¾ tsp flaky salt** and optional **¼ tsp maple extract**. Immediately spread onto the warm lined tray. Sprinkle with the remaining **¾ tsp rosemary** and **¾ tsp flaky salt**.

steps.title: Cool and break
steps.text: Leave until completely cold, at least **one hour**. Break into shards. Aim for a single layer of nuts with thin caramel between them. Check that a cooled piece snaps at room temperature; freezing a soft batch does not establish that it will hold at service.

steps.title: Assemble
steps.text: Select bite-sized shards and cut **10 g cheddar per selected shard**. Place the cheese on the broadest part just before serving. Keep the presentation to brittle and cheese, allowing the rosemary, salt and caramel to do the work.
steps.aside: This assembly and cheese portion are retained in the banked recipe; total cheese depends on the served count.

items: **Dry brittle** Cool fully, then store airtight at room temperature, separate from cheese. Bakerita gives **two to three weeks** for its original dry brittle and advises against refrigeration because moisture softens it. That is source guidance, not a tested shelf life for our optional-extract adaptation. Check the snap before service.
**Cheddar** Follow the actual product's refrigeration and opened-pack instructions. Cut only the amount needed for the selected shards; no storage life is assigned to assembled bites.
**Surplus** Keep unused dry shards in their labelled airtight container. Record finished weight and usable shard count before deciding how much of the batch to serve.

recipes.title: Buckwheat blini
recipes.subtitle: Horseradish cream and beetroot pickle
batch: **Batch:** one quarter-size source batch of blini, one quarter-size pickle batch and a small cream batch. Make blini about 4–5 cm across. **Predicted yield is about 22–28 mini pancakes** at 1½ tsp batter each (estimated from the batter volume, unmeasured), enough for 2 per guest with spares. Count the finished mini pancakes and measure the pickle yield, both TBD. Eight guests are confirmed; the number to serve per guest remains open. Freeze spare plain blini separately.

items: **Blini station.** Set out scales, measuring spoons, two bowls, a whisk, a non-stick frying pan, a thin spatula, a cooling rack and freezer containers with parchment. Separate **1 large egg** into two small bowls and beat each lightly; you need **half the yolk and half the white**, weighed (about 9 g yolk and 16 g white for a typical large egg; use half of what you actually have). Keep the other half for another use. Weigh **40 g buckwheat flour, 85 g warm water, 4 g skimmed milk powder, 28 g milk and 14 g butter**. Use warm water that feels comfortably warm to the touch.

**Pickle station.** Set out a saucepan, bowl of cold water, peeler, sharp knife, board, small bowl and shallow cooling/storage container. Wash **140 g small fresh beetroot** (about two), leaving roots and short stalks attached. Have **¼ eating apple and ¼ banana shallot** ready. Measure **56 ml water**, divided into **12 ml for the slurry and 44 ml for the pickle**.

**Cream and assembly station.** Set out a bowl, spoon or piping bag and a slotted spoon. Keep **60 g thick crème fraîche and 12 g prepared horseradish** refrigerated until needed. Verify gluten status of buckwheat flour, yeast, cornflour and prepared horseradish, and use clean equipment.

steps.text: Mix **40 g buckwheat flour, 85 g warm water, 4 g milk powder and ⅜ tsp instant yeast**. Cover and rest 30–60 minutes.
Whisk **the half egg yolk (about 9 g), 28 g milk, ¼ tsp sugar and ⅛ tsp salt** together. Stir into the sponge. Cover for 30–45 minutes.
Stir in **14 g melted butter**. Whisk **the half egg white (about 16 g)** to soft peaks in a small bowl with a fork or mini whisk, then fold it in.

Lightly oil the pan over medium heat. Portion **1½ tsp batter** per pancake, aiming for 4–5 cm rounds. Turn when the rims set and surface bubbles remain open. Cook the other side until golden and set. Cool on the rack, then pack with parchment between layers and freeze plain.

Cover **140 g whole beetroot** with cold water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, checking early if the beetroot are very small, then drain and cool in cold water. Rub off the skins and cut into **4–5 mm dice**. Toss with **¼ diced apple, ¼ diced banana shallot and ¼ tsp sea salt**.
Mix **½ tsp cornflour, 12 ml water and a small pinch of black pepper** into a smooth slurry.
Dissolve **19 g sugar** in **44 ml cider vinegar and the remaining 44 ml water** over low heat. Stir in the slurry and bring to a gentle simmer until slightly thickened.

Add all the beetroot/apple/shallot mixture. Simmer gently until the beetroot is cooked through but the cubes retain their shape. Allow about 3–5 minutes; use tenderness as the endpoint. Cool promptly in a shallow container and refrigerate at **4°C**.

Stir **60 g crème fraîche with 6 g prepared horseradish**. Taste with a little pickle. Add up to **6 g more horseradish** for a clear warming finish, and salt to taste. Cover and refrigerate at **4°C**.

Thaw the needed plain blini covered in the fridge. Serve thawed, or reheat at **150°C conventional / 130°C fan** until hot throughout, checking early because these are small. Let excess heat escape before topping. Keep cream and pickle refrigerated while the blini warm.

Spoon or pipe a little horseradish cream onto each blini. Add a small mound of pickle with a slotted spoon, leaving excess liquid behind. Keep enough glaze to coat the cubes. Serve promptly. Begin with roughly **½ tsp cream and 1 tsp pickle per blini**, adjusting to the actual pancake size. These serving amounts are working suggestions.

items: **Plain blini:** cool within two hours and freeze in an airtight container with parchment between layers. King Arthur supports up to one month frozen for its blini. Thaw covered in the fridge. If reheating, heat through until steaming, then allow excess heat to escape before topping. Reheat only once.

**Pickle:** prepare within two days of serving. Cool within two hours, cover and refrigerate at 4°C. This adaptation uses ordinary prepared-food handling. Its long-term preserving performance has not been established.
**Cream:** mix within two days of serving, keep covered at 4°C and follow any shorter ingredient-pack instructions. Reserve unused cream with clean utensils.

**Assembly:** keep all three components separate until needed. Reheat only the blini required. Discard any reheated blini remaining after service. Refrigerated pickle and cream retain their original two-day preparation limit. Label each batch with its preparation date.

recipes.title: Pressed rösti squares
recipes.subtitle: Trout pâté and salmon roe
recipes.makes: Up to 36 squares from batch B, 25 from batch A (targets)
batch: **For Daniela's current batch, use column B throughout the potato steps.** It uses all **1,056 g grated, par-cooked potato** in the available **23 × 23 × 5 cm tin**. Potato preparation is already complete, so start at step 4 if the potato is cold and grated. Do not add binder or butter again if already incorporated. Column A retains the banked 750 g reference batch.
**Internal tin base** A, reference batch: 20 × 20 cm, at least 3 cm deep; B, current measured batch: 23 × 23 cm, 5 cm deep
**Grated, par-cooked potato** A, reference batch: 750 g; B, current measured batch: 1,056 g
**Packed depth before baking** A, reference batch: About 1.8 cm; B, current measured batch: About 1.9 cm
**Finished depth after pressing** A, reference batch: About 1.5 cm, predicted; B, current measured batch: About 1.5–1.6 cm, predicted
**Added pressing load, after baking only** A, reference batch: About 1.3 kg; B, current measured batch: About 1.7 kg, calculated to preserve load per base area
**Cutting guide** A, reference batch: Trim to 17.5 cm square, then 5 × 5 pieces at 3.5 cm; B, current measured batch: If the slab permits, trim to 21 cm square, then 6 × 6 pieces at 3.5 cm

**Yield** A targets 25 squares; B could give 36 at the stated cutting dimensions, before any pieces rejected for breakage. Both are geometric targets, not measured yields. Do not trim away sound potato just to achieve a fixed border. If the cold slab is smaller, retain 3.5 cm pieces and accept fewer pieces or offcuts.

**Topping batch** The pâté and **30 g roe** below remain the reference allowance for **25 topped squares**, not an automatic increase for B's possible 36. Select up to 25 squares to top from this allowance and keep other potato squares separate.. The approximately 195 g pâté batch includes a margin for the processor and piping bag at about 6 g per square.

setup.heading: Paper, cover and pressing setup
items: **Paper A, the tin liner.** Use oven-rated baking parchment, not waxed paper. For B, cut a sheet about **40 × 40 cm**; for A, about **35 × 35 cm**. Crease it into the base and up all four sides, folding excess neatly at the corners. Leave at least **3 cm above two opposite rims** to grip later. Paper A stays under the potato throughout baking, pressing and chilling, and lifts the cold slab out.

**Paper B, the separate top sheet.** Cut a square just smaller than the internal base, about **22.5 × 22.5 cm for B**, or **19.5 × 19.5 cm for A**. This lies directly on the buttered potato surface during the covered bake. It is separate from Paper A's overhang. Remove it for the uncovered bake, then reuse it for pressing if intact and clean; otherwise cut a replacement of the same size.

**Foil cover.** Have a sheet large enough to seal across the tin rim over Paper B during the covered bake. It is not the pressing plate. No second tin or weights go in the oven in this clarified method.

**Pressing plate, for use after baking only.** Use a clean, rigid, flat insert just smaller than the base, about **22.5 cm square for B** or **19.5 cm square for A**. It must reach the potato surface without catching on the sides or bridging the rim. A small flat tray or board that fits is suitable. Alternatively, make a firm foil-wrapped cardboard insert. Keep any board/cardboard out of the oven. The two narrow tins listed in the source do not cover the square slab evenly.

**Weights.** Weigh closed food cans or another stable clean load to about **1.7 kg for B**, or **1.3 kg for A**, and distribute it across the pressing plate after baking. Do not balance a tall stack. Clear fridge space for the tin plus plate and load.

setup.heading: Potato station
items: Box grater with coarse holes, scales, large mixing bowl, fork, small bowls, pastry brush and a flat-bottomed measuring cup for initial packing.
For parboiling only, saucepan, skewer, rack and shallow cooling container. This stage is already done for the current measured batch.

Weigh the starch, mix salt, lightly beaten egg white and melted clarified butter from the chosen column below. Keep **mix butter**, **liner butter** and **top butter** in separate bowls so none is counted twice.
Use a middle oven shelf, with room for the foil cover. Preheat to **200°C conventional / 180°C fan** when ready to bake.

setup.heading: Cutting, pâté and finishing station
items: Sharp knife, ruler, board, hot-water jug and wiping cloth. Freezer trays lined with **additional baking parchment**, plus a rigid freezer container and parchment for separating layers. This tray paper is extra material, not Paper A or B.
Small processor or blender, spatula, lemon grater, scales and a piping bag with a **1 cm plain round nozzle**. An open star nozzle may be used only if the smooth pâté passes through it easily.

Fryer or suitable deep heavy saucepan, oil thermometer, slotted spoon and wire rack over a tray. Use the appliance's permitted oil level and capacity. **About 1.5 litres oil is an allowance, not a direction to pour that quantity into every pan.** Use fresh oil and equipment reserved for gluten-free food.
Keep the trout, dairy, pâté and roe refrigerated until their step; use a clean spoon for the roe. Check the actual packaged products against the recorded coeliac requirement.

method.heading: Parboil and chill, skip if already cold and grated

steps.title: Start cold
steps.text: For A, put **1 kg whole floury potatoes** into **1 litre cold water and 10 g salt**, adding more salted water only as described above if needed to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer.

steps.title: Parcook
steps.text: A skewer should pass through the outer 1–1.5 cm but still meet firm resistance in the centre. The established estimate is **10–15 minutes from simmering**, checking from 8 minutes for 150–200 g potatoes. Size and variety affect this; they should not be fully tender yet.

steps.title: Chill
steps.text: Drain onto a rack, let steam escape, then refrigerate promptly and within **two hours of cooking**. Cover once cooled. Keep at **4°C**.
steps.aside: Chill until cold right through, the master's **at least six hours or overnight** texture allowance. Cooling/storage guidance is the source, texture time is an untested recipe choice.

steps.title: Prepare the potato
steps.text: If not already grated, peel the chilled potatoes and grate coarsely into strands. Weigh **750 g for A** or use the measured **1,056 g for B**. Exclude any mushy pieces rather than working them into paste. If your batch is already mixed, skip step 5 rather than adding ingredients twice.

steps.title: Bind
steps.text: Toss the potato with **20 g starch + 7 g mix salt for A**, or **28.5 g starch + 9.5 g mix salt for B**, and the optional pinch of white pepper. Once no patches of dry starch remain, toss through **25 g egg white + 27 g mix butter for A**, or **34 g egg white + 38 g mix butter for B**. Coat evenly without kneading or mashing.

steps.title: Pack
steps.text: Brush Paper A inside the tin with **13 g liner butter for A**, or **18 g for B**. Add all the chosen batch. Press firmly into an even layer, including the corners, with the flat-bottomed cup. Target **about 1.8 cm for A**, or **about 1.9 cm for B**. Brush the surface with **13 g top butter for A**, or **18 g for B**. Judge actual depth with a ruler; the depth calculation is not a measured density guarantee.

steps.title: Bake covered, no weights
steps.text: Place **Paper B directly on the potato**. Seal the tin rim with the foil cover. Bake on the middle shelf at **200°C conventional / 180°C fan**, initially about **35 minutes**, an estimate. The layer order is tin → Paper A → potato → Paper B → foil. Do not put the pressing plate or cans in the oven.

steps.title: Finish uncovered
steps.text: Remove the foil and Paper B, keeping Paper A in place. Set Paper B aside on a clean surface. Bake uncovered for an estimated **15–20 minutes more**. The surface should be pale gold, the edges sizzling, and a thin knife in the centre should meet no firm/raw potato resistance. If still firm, continue and check again; these times are not a deadline. Deep browning is reserved for frying. No shorter or longer duration has been validated for B or the revised cover.

steps.title: Fit the press after baking
steps.text: Rest the tin for about **10 minutes**, then return Paper B to the potato surface. Put the fitted pressing plate on Paper B, followed by the evenly distributed **1.3 kg load for A**, or **1.7 kg for B**. The plate must contact the slab across its surface, not rest on the tin rim. Let excess steam escape, then refrigerate promptly, always within **two hours of leaving the oven**. Keep the tin on a stable fridge shelf at **4°C**, with the weights in place, for **at least eight hours or overnight**. Do not wait on the counter for the slab to become completely cold. The cold slab should be flat and firm with no springy give.

steps.title: Unmould
steps.text: Remove the weights, pressing plate and Paper B. Use Paper A's overhang to lift the cold slab onto a board. If it catches, ease the paper away from the tin sides before lifting. Turn the slab over, then peel off Paper A. The smooth face that touched the tin liner is now uppermost and is the serving face.

steps.title: Cut to size
steps.text: Measure the actual slab. For A, a **17.5 × 17.5 cm trimmed square** gives a **5 × 5 grid of 3.5 cm pieces**. For B, a **21 × 21 cm trimmed square** gives a **6 × 6 grid of 3.5 cm pieces**, if the cold slab is large enough. These are cutting plans, not guaranteed yields. Trim only what is needed to square off ragged edges, retaining offcuts. Mark cuts with a ruler, then press the knife straight down. Dip the blade in hot water and wipe it dry between cuts.

steps.title: Freeze the pieces and test offcuts
steps.text: Place the squares and two offcuts on the additional parchment-lined freezer trays, smooth face up, about **1 cm apart**. Freeze uncovered until hard throughout, an estimated **2–3 hours**, with time dependent on the freezer. They must be solid, not merely crusted outside.

steps.title: Check cohesion using the offcuts
steps.text: Once hard, fry the two frozen offcuts using steps 20–21. Check that they hold together and become hot through the centre. If they split, stop using the deep-fry method and use the oven fallback for the remaining squares. This check happens during preparation; it is not a separate recipe trial.

steps.title: Pack the frozen squares
steps.text: Lift them off the tray paper and put them in a rigid freezer container, smooth side up, separating layers with additional parchment. Close and label with recipe name, preparation date and **fry from frozen**. Remove excess air only if using bags, without crushing the pieces. Keep frozen until needed; do not thaw before frying.

steps.title: Blend the fish
steps.text: Blend **100 g hot-smoked trout**, **7 ml lemon juice**, **zest of ⅓ lemon**, the **generous pinch of cayenne** and **pinch of white pepper** until no visible fish flakes remain. Scrape down as needed.

steps.title: Add dairy
steps.text: Add **65 g cold cream cheese** and **20 g cold crème fraîche**.
steps.aside: Pulse briefly until smooth, stopping as soon as combined; **10–15 seconds** was the master's estimate, not a required duration.

steps.title: Adjust piping texture
steps.text: It should hold a soft peak on a spatula. If too stiff to pipe, add reserve crème fraîche in **5 g additions, up to 10 g extra total**. Do not pour in the full reserve automatically.

steps.title: Season with the finish in mind
steps.text: Taste a small amount with a few grains of roe. Add a few drops of the reserve lemon juice if needed and fine salt only if still needed. No extra horseradish is included in this pâté.

steps.title: Chill and bag
steps.text: Cover and refrigerate at **4°C**. Transfer cold pâté into the bag fitted with the **1 cm nozzle**, close the top and return to the fridge. It should hold a piped rosette when cold. Bagging does not restart its storage time; use within **two days of making** and within any shorter ingredient use-by/opened limits.

method.heading: Fry and top only the squares being served

steps.title: Set up
steps.text: Heat the fresh frying oil to **180°C**, using the appliance's permitted fill. The approximately **1.5 litres** is stock to have available, not an instruction to exceed that fill. Remove only the squares needed for this round; keep the others frozen. Tap off loose frost. Keep the pâté and the **30 g roe allowance** refrigerated until topping, and return reserves between rounds.

steps.title: Fry from frozen
steps.text: Lower a small batch gently into the oil. The master suggests **6–8 pieces**, but use fewer if crowding or the oil temperature falls below about **170°C**. Fry for an estimated **3–4 minutes**, turning once, until deep golden and hot throughout. Break open a test piece to check the centre; colour alone is insufficient. Bring the oil back to **180°C** before another batch.
steps.aside: These fry times remain untested for the actual batch.

steps.title: Drain
steps.text: Lift onto the wire rack, smooth face up, and add a light sprinkle of flaky salt. The tray underneath catches oil; the potato rests on the rack, not paper.

steps.title: Top and serve
steps.text: Let the hard steaming subside, about **1–2 minutes** as a working cue. Pipe **about 6 g cold pâté per selected square**. Divide the **30 g roe allowance across up to 25 selected squares**, about **1.2 g each if using all 25**, and add the optional finely snipped chives. Do not scale the pâté or roe automatically to B's possible 36 pieces. Serve promptly; there is no established hold once topped.

notes: **Oven fallback, if pieces split or frying is impractical** Put frozen pieces on a rack over a tray in a **220°C conventional / 200°C fan oven** and turn once, cooking until deep golden and hot throughout. No duration is established. This remains an untested fallback, with a less crisp result predicted. Keep toppings off until after cooking and the brief resting cue.

items: **Potato components** Refrigerate promptly and within two hours after each cooking stage. Cover once cooled; keep at 4°C. Complete the recipe's cold stages and freeze the cut pieces promptly rather than extending fridge holds. Prepared-food guidance is a maximum two-day refrigerated hold, not an extra two days granted at each step.
**Frozen squares** Keep frozen until frying. Longer freezer quality has not been assessed for this adapted recipe; freeze hard before packing and use the prepared batch for this dinner.
**Pâté** Keep covered at 4°C and use within two days of making or an earlier ingredient limit. Keep separate from potato; do not freeze this pâté as part of this recipe.
**Roe** Follow the jar's chilled-storage and opened-use instructions. Use a clean spoon and keep the reserve chilled.

**Partial batches and surplus** Untopped frozen squares can stay frozen for later rounds under the same handling plan. Fried topped squares are intended for immediate service; no leftover storage or reheating method is established for them.

recipes.title: Kimchi devilled eggs
batch: **Batch:** 8 eggs, making 16 filled halves, which is 2 per guest for eight guests with no spares. Eight guests are confirmed; the final serving count remains TBD.

items: Set out a saucepan that holds **8 large eggs** in one layer, an ice-water bowl, slotted spoon, knife, board, fine sieve, mini processor, spatula and piping bag with a broad plain nozzle.
Set out shallow covered containers for whites and filling. Clear space in the fridge at **4°C**.

Drain the kimchi, reserving **13 ml brine**. Weigh **55 g drained kimchi**, then chop finely. Divide **15 g for tasting/adjustment and 40 g for the topping**. Keep the tasting portion separate from the garnish.
Check the actual kimchi, mayonnaise and gochujang labels for coeliac suitability. Use bought mayonnaise. Kimchi flavour and heat vary, so season the filling with the actual garnish.

steps.title: Cook the eggs
steps.text: Lower **8 eggs** into gently boiling water. Cook for about 10 minutes, checking that whites and yolks are firm. Transfer immediately to ice water. Once cold, peel and halve lengthways. Put all **8 yolks** in the processor and refrigerate the **16 white halves**, covered.

steps.title: Blend the filling
steps.text: Process the **8 yolks, 40 g mayonnaise, 7 g gochujang and 7 ml kimchi brine** until smooth. Scrape down the bowl. Taste a little filling with some of the reserved **15 g chopped kimchi**.

steps.title: Adjust in small additions
steps.text: Use up to **15 g more mayonnaise** for a creamier texture, up to **6 g more gochujang** for heat, and up to **6 ml more brine** for acidity and loosening. Aim for a smooth mixture that holds a soft mound. Salt only if needed. Keep the chopped kimchi separate so the filling stays smooth.

steps.title: Refrigerate separately
steps.text: Transfer the filling to its covered container or piping bag. Keep it, the covered egg whites and the **40 g garnish kimchi** refrigerated at **4°C** until assembly.

steps.title: Fill and garnish
steps.text: Pipe the filling evenly into the **16 white halves**. Share the **40 g garnish kimchi** between them, then finish with the sliced green parts of **2 spring onions** and **1½ tsp toasted sesame seeds** across the batch. Keep the egg white rims clear so each half can be picked up neatly.

items: Prepare the whites and filling the day before and refrigerate separately. Pipe and garnish for service.
Cool cooked components promptly, within two hours, and keep at 4°C. Use within two days of preparation, or any shorter ingredient-pack limit. Return reserve portions to refrigeration promptly.
Keep hard-cooked egg whites refrigerated. FoodSafety.gov advises against freezing hard-cooked eggs.
Label containers with the preparation date and follow the kimchi/mayonnaise pack's opened-use instructions. Prepared components keep their original preparation limit after assembly.

recipes.title: Salmon hand roll
recipes.subtitle: Yuzu rice, yuzu-daikon pickle, wasabi furikake
batch: **Working batch: 10 open hand rolls**, for 8 confirmed guests plus 2 spares or tests. Final count TBD.

**Per roll (working amounts):** 15 g yuzu rice, 25 g zuke salmon, 5 g salted cucumber, 4 g yuzu-daikon pickle, 2 g yuzu-kosho mayonnaise (optional), 0.5 g wasabi, 1 g wasabi furikake, 1 nori sheet (size TBD: half or quarter sheet to suit the holder).
The rice and pickle batches make more than 10 rolls need, so you can taste and adjust. Weigh and record the cooked rice and drained pickle.

items: **Day before or morning (pickle):**
Set out a small pan, a fine sieve, a jar or lidded container (glass preferred), a bowl for the brine, a knife or julienne peeler, scales and kitchen paper.

**Check labels** for wheat, barley or malt in the tamari, mirin, rice vinegar, yuzu juice, yuzu kosho, wasabi, mayonnaise, nori, kombu and wasabi furikake. If a label is unknown, don't use it for the coeliac guest.
**Service day (rice, salmon, assembly):**

Set out the rice pot, a wide bowl or sushi tub, a rice paddle, a fan and a damp cloth. For the fish, set out a board and knife used only for raw fish, a non-reactive tray, cling film and kitchen paper.
Keep the nori sealed with a desiccant until plating. Have 10 holders, 10 plates and small bowls for the wasabi and furikake within reach.

method.heading: Pickle (at least 3 hours ahead; proposed: the day before)

steps.title: Make the kombu dashi
steps.text: Soak **1 piece of kombu (about 5 × 3 cm)** in **100 ml water** for 15–30 min. Heat on medium-low until it just simmers, then turn off the heat. Measure out **90 ml dashi**, topping up with water if needed.

steps.title: Season the amazu
steps.text: While the dashi is warm, stir in **50 g sugar** and **½ tsp salt** until dissolved. Add **120 ml rice vinegar** and **¼ to ½ dried chilli**. Leave to cool.

steps.title: Brine the daikon
steps.text: Dissolve **1 tbsp salt** in **500 ml water**. Add **150 g daikon matchsticks** and leave for about 30 min.

steps.title: Squeeze
steps.text: Drain, then squeeze the daikon firmly by hand in small handfuls. This keeps it crisp and stops it wetting the nori.

steps.title: Pickle
steps.text: Put the daikon and the **julienned peel of ¼ yuzu** in the jar. Pour over the cooled amazu, loosen any clumps and refrigerate for **at least 2–3 hours**. Taste: it should be crisp, sharp-sweet and clearly citrus.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Wash **1 go (180 ml) rice** and cook it slightly firm, with a little less water than the packet says, adding **1 piece of kombu (about 5 cm)**. Remove the kombu when the rice is cooked.

steps.title: Make the awase-zu
steps.text: While the rice cooks, stir **17 ml rice vinegar**, **8 ml yuzu juice**, **1 tbsp (15 ml) sugar**, **3 g salt** and **5 g minced ginger** until the sugar and salt dissolve.

steps.title: Season
steps.text: Weigh the hot rice into a wide bowl and note the weight. Pour the awase-zu down the paddle, about **1 ml for every 10 g of rice**, so all of it for about 330 g. Mix up from the bottom, then cut sideways with the paddle until the rice is glossy with no lumps.

steps.title: Cool and hold
steps.text: Fan the rice and turn it until it reaches **body temperature**. Cover with a damp cloth and keep at room temperature. **Don't refrigerate it**, as that hardens the rice. A safe holding time is not verified; plan to use it the same session.

steps.title: Make the tare
steps.text: Bring **15 ml mirin** and **15 ml sake** to the boil to cook off the alcohol. Cool, then stir in **30 ml tamari**, **1.5 to 2 g yuzu kosho** and **1 to 2 ml sesame oil**. Add **1 piece of kombu (about 5 × 5 cm)** and chill. Proposed: steep the kombu for at least 30 min, then remove it.

steps.title: Cut
steps.text: On the raw-fish board, trim and cut **250 g salmon** into strips about **5 mm thick, 1 cm wide and 6 cm long** (proposed). You should get about 4 strips per roll.

steps.title: Rinse
steps.text: Mix **400 ml iced water**, **100 g ice** and **1 tbsp salt** until the salt dissolves. Dip the strips, stir 3–4 times, leave for **1 min**, then lift out and pat thoroughly dry with kitchen paper. The rinse must be ice-cold.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.text: Lay the **250 g salmon** in one layer in a non-reactive tray. Pour over the tare, press cling film onto the surface and chill for **about 25 min**. Taste a strip at 20 min. 20–40 min is the usual range for salmon; too long makes it salty, firm and dry.

steps.title: Drain
steps.text: Lift out the strips, blot them on kitchen paper and keep chilled on a tray. Discard the tare.

steps.title: Salt the cucumber
steps.text: Toss **50 g cucumber matchsticks** with **about 0.5 g salt**. Leave for about 5 min, until water appears, then squeeze gently and blot.

steps.title: Yuzu-kosho mayonnaise (optional)
steps.text: Stir **20 g mayonnaise** with **0.5 to 1 g yuzu kosho** until smooth. Keep chilled.

steps.title: Drain the pickle
steps.text: Lift out **40 g yuzu-daikon pickle**, with some of the peel, and blot it.

method.heading: Assemble (last thing before serving)

steps.text: Lay **1 nori sheet** on each holder. For the prototype, test **1 lettuce strip** on some sheets.
Place **15 g rice** in a narrow strip along one side of the sheet, not spread across it.
On the rice, lay **5 g cucumber** and **4 g pickle**, then a small dot of **2 g yuzu-kosho mayonnaise** if using, then **25 g salmon strips** running along the fold line.
Add **0.5 g wasabi** and **kaiware** if using. Finish with **1 g wasabi furikake** and serve at once.

notes: **Totals for 10 rolls:** rice 15 g × 10 = 150 g, from about 330 g cooked. Salmon 25 g × 10 = 250 g. Cucumber 5 g × 10 = 50 g. Pickle 4 g × 10 = 40 g, from the larger batch. Mayonnaise 2 g × 10 = 20 g. Wasabi 0.5 g × 10 = 5 g. Furikake 1 g × 10 = 10 g.

items: **Rice:** room temperature under a damp cloth, not refrigerated. Holding time is unverified.

**Pickle:** the source gives about a week refrigerated for its turnip amazu pickle. The keeping time of this daikon adaptation is **unverified**. The amazu base on its own keeps about six months chilled.

**Salmon:** marinate close to service. Make-ahead storage is **unverified; don't adopt one**. No marinade or rinse here is a safety step, and vinegar, soy and wasabi don't kill anisakis. Raw-fish safety depends on Daniela's supplier.
**Nori:** sealed with a desiccant until plating. How long it stays crisp under the toppings is TBD.

recipes.title: Celeriac and Jerusalem artichoke soup
recipes.subtitle: Fried sage and parsley oil
batch: **Portions:** 10–12 × **200 ml**, for **8 confirmed guests** plus leftovers. Finished-volume target **2–2.4 litres**, aiming for 2.4 litres; actual yield to be measured. Eight bowls use 1.6 litres, leaving a target 400–800 ml.

items: Set up only the stage you are cooking now. The soup base, parsley oil and dinner finishing each have their own setup below. Keep the milk refrigerated until needed.

setup.heading: Soup-base station
items: **Clear the workspace.** Put out a chopping board, sharp knife, peeler, scales, measuring jug, small bowls, a bowl of cold water for the artichokes and a bowl for peelings. Have a clean cloth ready.

**Set out the cooking kit.** Place the lidded saucepan on the hob, with a spatula or wooden spoon beside it. Have the stick blender, a tasting spoon and the fine sieve ready. If freezing, put shallow containers, lids, labels and a marker within reach and clear space for cooling and storage.

**Prepare the ingredients before turning on the heat.** Peel, weigh and finely slice **600 g celeriac and 400 g artichokes**. Keep the artichokes briefly in the cold water, then drain before cooking. Slice **330 g shallots and 3 garlic cloves** and put them together in one bowl. Weigh **80 g butter**, measure **1,250 ml prepared vegetable stock** and put **½ tsp salt** beside the stove. The stock quantity is prepared stock, not concentrate.

**Keep the finishing ingredients separate.** The **400 ml milk and 25 ml lemon juice** belong to finishing, not to the base going into the freezer. Label the base containers with the fraction stored and the corresponding finishing amounts.

setup.heading: Parsley-oil station
items: Have **25 g washed parsley with tender stalks**, **100 ml light olive oil** and the optional extra **50 ml oil** ready. Set out a small saucepan for blanching, a colander, the small blender jug, a sieve lined with clean muslin over a bowl, and a clean lidded jar with a label. Check that the blender can process this small quantity. Set up the strainer before blanching so the finished oil has somewhere to go.

setup.heading: Dinner finishing and plating station
items: Have the thawed base and the correctly scaled milk ready; keep the portion intended for leftovers separate before reheating. For the whole batch, measure **400 ml milk**, **15 ml lemon juice** and a separate **10 ml lemon juice** for adjustment. Put salt, pepper, a tasting spoon and a little hot water or stock within reach.

Pat **16 sage leaves** thoroughly dry for the eight dinner bowls and arrange them in **two groups of 8**. Measure the frying oil into **two 15 ml portions**. Set out the small frying pan, tongs and a plate lined with kitchen paper.

Arrange **8 soup bowls**, a ladle, a measuring jug to check the **200 ml portion**, a small spoon or dropper for the parsley oil and a clean cloth for the rims. Set aside about **10 ml parsley oil** for those bowls; keep the rest refrigerated. Have the bowls warm when ready to plate.

For dinner, fry **16 sage leaves** in two batches of 8; leave the remaining **8 leaves** unfried for later portions. The intended soup texture is silky and flowing, with the garnishes as restrained accents.

steps.title: Check your mise en place
steps.text: Have **600 g peeled, finely sliced celeriac and 400 g peeled, finely sliced artichokes** ready as above. Drain the artichokes before cooking. The preparation allowance covers this once, not again here.

steps.title: Soften the aromatics
steps.text: Melt **80 g butter** over medium-low heat. Add **330 g shallots, 3 sliced garlic cloves and ½ tsp salt**. Cook gently until soft, keeping the garlic pale. Cook to softness; about 8 minutes is a smaller-batch reference, so this batch may differ.

steps.title: Cook the roots
steps.text: Add **600 g celeriac and 400 g artichokes**. Stir gently until the edges begin to soften and take a little colour. Aim for light golden edges rather than deep browning; about 10 minutes is a smaller-batch reference.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.text: Add **1,250 ml vegetable stock**, bring to a gentle simmer and cover. Start checking after 20 minutes and continue until both roots crush readily against the pan with a spoon. Add a little hot water if needed to prevent catching. Roughly 15–30 minutes, but the larger batch may differ: cook to tenderness, not a compulsory hour.

steps.title: Blend
steps.text: Blend thoroughly with a stick blender until silky. Pass through a fine sieve if needed to remove persistent fibres. Keep the **400 ml milk and 25 ml lemon juice** out for now. For advance preparation, cool and store the base as below; otherwise continue to finishing.

steps.title: Blanch and blend
steps.text: Blanch **25 g parsley** in lightly salted boiling water for **30 seconds**. Drain thoroughly, then blend with **100 ml light olive oil** in a small jug until finely processed. If needed, add some of the reserved **50 ml oil**, a little at a time, to blend or soften the intensity. The proposed cue is a clean parsley flavour without an aggressively bitter oil finish.

steps.title: Strain
steps.text: Let the oil drain through a muslin-lined sieve into a clean container without pressing the solids. Cover, date and refrigerate. Make up to **3 days ahead**; use within that period. This follows the oil recipe and stays within the general four-day refrigerated limit for homemade herb oils.

steps.title: Warm and add milk
steps.text: If frozen, thaw the base in the fridge. For the **whole batch**, warm gently, stir in **400 ml whole milk**, and heat until steaming hot throughout, stirring well. Bring just to a gentle simmer, without prolonged boiling. If reheating only part, add the same fraction of the **400 ml milk** and reserve the rest for the stored base.

steps.title: Balance the flavour and texture
steps.text: Off the heat, add **15 ml lemon juice** and black pepper. Taste before adding any of the remaining **10 ml lemon juice** or more salt. Aim for a savoury soup lifted by acidity, without tasting distinctly lemony. Loosen with hot water or stock only as needed for a flowing consistency; briefly blend again if necessary. For a partial batch, scale the lemon quantities by the same fraction as the milk.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: Record the finished volume. The target is **2–2.4 litres**, not a measured yield guarantee. Do not dilute a well-balanced soup simply to hit the number. Keep any surplus; do not reduce it solely to fit 12 portions. If reserving leftovers, separate that share of base before reheating and scale its finishing ingredients accordingly.

steps.title: Crisp the sage
steps.text: Heat **15 ml olive oil** in a small frying pan over medium heat. Add **8 thoroughly dry sage leaves** for the dinner service, or **12** if serving all 12 portions, provided they fit without crowding. Fry until crisp, about **2 minutes**, then drain on kitchen paper. Repeat with the remaining **15 ml oil** and **8 or 12 leaves**. Use the crisp-leaf cue rather than waiting for dark browning.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Ladle **200 ml hot soup** into each warm bowl. Dot about **¼ tsp (1.25 ml) parsley oil** over the surface and add **2 crisp sage leaves** immediately before serving. Leave most of the pale soup visible; the garnish should complement the roots. For eight bowls this uses **1.6 litres soup, about 10 ml parsley oil and 16 sage leaves**.

items: **Soup:** cool promptly in shallow containers, using a cold-water bath and stirring if useful, and refrigerate or freeze within 2 hours. Keep refrigerated at 4 °C or below and use within 2 days, or freeze for up to 3 months under the existing general guidance. Freeze the base before adding milk and lemon; butter remains in the base. Thaw in the fridge and reheat only the amount needed, until steaming hot throughout. Reheat once. These are practical handling instructions, not a guarantee of frozen texture.

**Labels:** note the stored fraction and its finishing ingredients. Half a base batch takes **200 ml milk** and **7.5 ml lemon juice initially, plus up to 5 ml**; the whole batch takes **400 ml milk** and **15 ml + up to 10 ml lemon juice**.
**Parsley oil:** refrigerate immediately after making, use within 3 days, and keep the main container chilled while using a small serving amount. Do not store at room temperature.
**Sage:** fry close to plating. Leave leaves for leftover soup unfried; no crisp-storage promise is made.

recipes.title: Turkey crown roulade
recipes.subtitle: Guanciale, chestnut, mushroom and apple
batch: **Batch:** two rolls, one per **2.2 kg breast-on-bone crown** (4.4 kg total before removing skin and bones). There is no back to remove or reserve. Keep each crown’s two breast halves and skin together for its roll. Dinner is for eight guests overall, with a separate pescatarian main. Portion the turkey for the number of turkey plates at the pass. **Proposed plating allowance:** 150 g cooked roulade per turkey plate alongside mash and sides. Measure the cooked yield before counting spare portions.

**Scale by meat weight.** After deboning, weigh each crown’s trimmed breast meat for its roll, excluding skin, bones and any removed tenderloins. Multiply the per-kilo quantities by the weight of the meat in kilograms. The **4.4 kg bone-in purchase weight must not be used as the filling multiplier**. The table’s **3 kg trimmed-meat column is only an arithmetic example**, not the predicted yield of these crowns. Use the actual weights to size the batch. Record crown A and B trimmed breast weights separately, then their total. Combine the filling ingredients for both rolls if convenient and divide the cooked filling in proportion to each roll’s meat weight, keeping a little back if it would make either roll hard to close.

items: **Turkey station:** a raw-poultry board, boning knife, scales, covered tray, paper towels, ruler and kitchen twine. If the butcher debones the crowns, ask for the breast halves, skin and bones packed separately by crown, with as much intact skin as possible. Check whether the turkey is already salted, brined or injected. Keep the turkey refrigerated at **4°C** until needed. Before starting this raw-freezing route, check the use-by date, prior freezing/thawing history and supplier instructions, including suitability for home freezing. If the crowns arrive frozen or previously thawed, resolve those instructions before assembling for freezing.

**Filling station:** a clean board and knife, wide frying pan, spatula and shallow dish for cooling. Weigh the scaled amounts from the table. Chop the mushrooms and shallots finely. Peel and core the tart apple and cut it into roughly 4–5 mm dice. Crush the reserved chestnuts with a fork and finely chop the rest. Strip the thyme leaves from their stems. Finely dice the guanciale, mince the garlic and have whole nutmeg and a fine grater ready. Set out a slotted spoon and a small heatproof dish for weighing rendered fat. The browned pork pieces stay in the filling for bite; no crisp garnish is needed.

**Freezing station:** freezer-rated food wrap, heavy freezer bags or foil, labels and a tray that fits the freezer. Check there is room for the two rolls without crushing them, and keep the cold filling and turkey refrigerated until assembly.

**Oven and carving station:** middle oven shelf, rimmed roasting tray with a rack, foil for shielding, a leave-in probe if available and a reliable instant-read thermometer to verify each roll. Check both rolls fit with space between them. Set out a clean carving board, sharp knife, scissors and scales.

The retained guanciale fat is part of the guanciale’s yield, not a second ingredient to buy. Use it in place of the former mushroom-base butter. Nutmeg remains a small spoon measure adjusted by taste, with no guessed conversion to grams. Porcini and a separate crisp-pork garnish are outside this finalised version.

steps.title: Separate the meat, skin and bones
steps.text: From each of the **2 × 2.2 kg breast-on-breastbone crowns**, ease off the skin in one sheet where possible. With the crown steady, follow the breastbone and any attached ribs closely with the boning knife to lift off the breast halves. Check for stray cartilage or bone fragments. Remove any loose tenderloins and reserve them for another use. Weigh the trimmed breast meat for each roll separately and scale the amounts above. Keep the meat and skin covered and refrigerated. Reserve the **2 breastbone frames**, any attached ribs/cartilage and meaty bone trimmings for the stock and demi. These are breast frames without backs. Weigh them together separately from the trimmed breast meat, and keep any supplied giblets separate. The stock recipe adds a proposed **2 kg whole chicken wings**; it no longer assumes two complete carcasses. Clean the poultry station before preparing other food.

steps.title: Render the guanciale and cook the aromatics
steps.text: Per kilo of trimmed breast meat, gently cook **30 g finely diced guanciale** over medium-low heat until its fat has released and the pieces are lightly golden with a little bite. Lift out and reserve all the browned pieces. Retain **10 g rendered fat per kg meat** in the pan and set any excess aside. If less than **10 g per kg** has rendered, add only enough **unsalted butter** to bring that base cooking fat to **10 g per kg**. This is separate from the apple butter. Add **45 g chopped shallot per kg** and cook until soft and gently golden. Add **160 g finely chopped mushrooms per kg**, working in batches if crowded. Cook until the liquid evaporates and the mushrooms develop browned patches. Add **2 g minced garlic and 2 g thyme leaves per kg**, cooking until the garlic smells mellow. The spatula should leave a clear trail without liquid running back into it.

steps.title: Sauté the apple and complete the filling
steps.text: Per kilo of meat, sauté **45 g diced tart apple in 6 g unsalted butter** in a separate pan until its edges soften, the dice hold their shape and no juice pools. Fold into the mushroom base with **60 g chopped cooked chestnuts and 20 g crushed cooked chestnuts per kg**, and all the reserved **browned guanciale pieces** from step 2. Add a little **freshly grated nutmeg**, starting with a **scant ⅛ tsp for the 3 kg meat illustration**, then **black pepper to taste**. Taste the completed cooked filling before it touches raw poultry, adding **salt only as needed** because the guanciale is already seasoned. Aim for a savoury filling with clear thyme, mild apple tang and background nutmeg warmth. It should hold together when pressed; the pork supplies bite, without needing to remain crisp. Spread in a shallow dish and chill promptly before rolling.

steps.title: Butterfly the breast portions
steps.text: For each roll, open the thick portions of both breast halves like a book and flatten thick spots gently, aiming for an even sheet about **1–1.5 cm thick** where practical. Lay the halves slightly overlapping to make a rectangle, offsetting the thick ends if that gives a more even sheet. Lay the meat against one edge of its reserved skin, skin side down, so you have spare skin to wrap around the outside. Season plain meat with **6 g fine salt per kg of trimmed breast** on the inside.

steps.title: Spread, roll and tie
steps.text: Share the chilled stuffing between the two crowns according to their trimmed meat weights. Spread a thin layer, about **5 mm** as a starting point, with roughly a **2 cm clear border**. Stop when the meat can roll without pushing stuffing out. Roll the meat snugly around the filling, keeping the skin on the outside, and pull the spare skin over the seam. Tie at about **3–4 cm intervals** and once along the length if needed to tuck the ends. Record each roll’s weight, widest diameter and trimmed breast weight, and reserve its **5 ml neutral oil and 2 g fine salt per kg of trimmed breast** for the roasting step. Freeze promptly as below, without an overnight hold of the assembled raw rolls in the fridge. For immediate cooking instead, go straight to step 8 with the oven preheated. Keep any unspread filling that has stayed separate from raw poultry in its own dish. Discard any excess from the raw-poultry station.

steps.title: Wrap and freeze raw
steps.text: Wrap each tied roll closely in freezer-rated food wrap, then put it into a heavy freezer bag or overwrap with freezer foil, excluding excess air. Keep the twine in place. Label **raw stuffed turkey, cook before eating**, with the assembly date, roll weight, diameter and reserved skin-seasoning quantities. Place seam down on a tray and freeze promptly at **−18°C or below**, keeping the rolls separate while they freeze. This recipe plans a one-week freeze, not a week of raw refrigerator storage.

steps.title: Thaw fully in the fridge
steps.text: Put each wrapped roll in a leakproof tray on the bottom shelf at **4°C**. Allow enough time for the centre to thaw fully; the general **24-hour** guide is not a promise for a large stuffed roll. Follow any stricter supplier instructions. Once fully thawed, cook and serve within **24 hours**. Remove all freezer wrapping before cooking, leaving only the kitchen twine. Do not use the roasting method below on a partly frozen roll.

steps.title: Dry, season, roast and verify both rolls
steps.text: Preheat to **175°C fan or 190°C conventional**. Pat the thawed skin thoroughly dry, brush each roll with its reserved **5 ml neutral oil per kg of trimmed breast** and season plain, unseasoned turkey skin with its reserved **2 g fine salt per kg**. Set seam down on the rack with space between the rolls. Roast on the middle shelf at **175°C fan or 190°C conventional**. If using a leave-in probe, place it near the centre of the larger roll to follow its progress. For each roll, use an instant-read thermometer to verify at least **75°C in the centre of the stuffing and in the thickest meat beside it**. Check more than one spot around the centre and use the lowest reading. Remove each roll as it passes both checks. If the skin browns too quickly, shield that area loosely with foil. If it needs more colour as the centre approaches the target, a brief, watched grill finish is optional. Verify both temperatures afterwards.

steps.title: Rest, carve and serve
steps.text: Rest each cooked roll uncovered for about **15 minutes**. Remove the twine and cut across the roll with a sharp knife. Use **about 150 g cooked roulade per turkey plate** as the working plating guide. Spoon the separate demi beside the slices to keep the skin crisp. Weigh the total cooked yield and note how cleanly the slices hold together.

items: **Filling ahead:** Make the filling separately if useful. Cool promptly in a shallow dish, cover and refrigerate at **4°C** within **2 hours**. For this master, make it up to the day before assembly. Use it cold, keep it separate from raw turkey until rolling, then follow the prompt raw-freezing route in steps 5–7. If cooking immediately instead, assemble only when the preheated oven is ready.

**After thawing:** roast the fully thawed rolls, rather than partially cooking and finishing later. The **75°C centre checks** in step 8 apply to the stuffing and meat of **each** roll. Raw freezing changes the preparation route, not these cooking checks.

**After dinner:** Portion leftover cooked roulade into small pieces or slices in shallow containers. Cool and refrigerate at **4°C** or freeze within **2 hours**. Use refrigerated leftovers within **2 days** or frozen leftovers within **3 months**. Thaw in the fridge. If serving hot, reheat only what you need once, until steaming hot throughout, and discard leftovers from that reheated portion. Expect softer skin after chilling.

recipes.title: Turkey stock and demi
recipes.subtitle: Roast stock, frozen as a sauce base
batch: Use the **breastbone frames and meaty bone trimmings from the two 2.2 kg crowns**, plus **2 kg whole chicken wings**. Include attached ribs/cartilage if present. Keep the skin required for the roulades with the breast meat; do not strip the wings of their skin or meat.

**Weigh the stock parts.** Add the turkey frames/trimmings weight to the **whole wings’ raw weight**, including their meat, skin, joints and bones. This combined weight is the multiplier for the aromatic table. For example, **2 kg wings + 1 kg turkey frames = 3 kg stock parts**; the 1 kg of frames is an arithmetic illustration, **not a yield estimate**. Record any giblets separately. The **4.4 kg original crown weight is not the stock-parts weight**.
**Confirmed serving allowance:** **100–120 ml finished sauce per turkey plate**. For **N turkey plates**, allow **100 × N to 120 × N ml**.

**Working batch target, not a measured yield:** approximately **1 litre finished sauce**. An eight-portion planning allowance needs **800–960 ml**, leaving **40–200 ml** from a 1 litre batch. Eight guests are confirmed overall, including a pescatarian main requirement; this is an upper planning allowance, not confirmation of eight turkey plates. Keep the poultry sauce separate from the pescatarian main. Confirm actual turkey plate count. The target is not a measured yield or a reason to sacrifice flavour/body.

Keep the banked **2 kg whole wings plus both turkey breast frames** as the stock starting point. Measure the strained stock and final sauce; more finished sauce does not mean automatically doubling the bones or diluting a finished demi without tasting. If the batch cannot provide the target volume at a pleasant hot coating, record the shortfall and make extra stock before service.

items: Set out the scales, enough rimmed roasting trays for a single layer of the wings and frames, a stockpot that can hold the broken-down parts, tongs, ladle, fine sieve, measuring jug, wide reduction pan and shallow cooling containers. Check pot and cooling capacity before cooking.

Check whether any giblets were supplied with these breast-only crowns; none are assumed. If present, use the **heart and cleaned gizzard**, plus **neck if included**. Reserve the **liver** for another preparation. Record what is supplied.

Break the turkey breast frames into pot-sized pieces or ask the butcher to do this. Separate the **2 kg whole wings** at their joints if useful for tray/pot fit, retaining the tips. Retain cartilage and meaty trim. Weigh the combined stock parts before scaling. Set aside the measured **onion, carrot and celery**, roughly chopped, with **thyme, bay and peppercorns**.

Have ice and cold water ready for cooling, along with clean freezer containers and labels. Suggested container sizes are **250–500 ml**, subject to capacity. Freeze the reduced base in labelled portions that together cover the working batch.
Deboning supplies the bones while the breast meat and skin go into the raw frozen roulades in the turkey roulade. Check the actual crown labels and freezing history before starting that route.

method.heading: Roast and extract the stock

steps.title: Brown the poultry parts
steps.text: Using the illustrative **3 kg combined stock-parts** batch, coat **2 kg whole chicken wings plus 1 kg turkey frames/trimmings with 30 ml oil**. For the actual batch, use **10 ml oil per kg of combined parts**. Spread in a single layer, using separate trays or batches as needed, and roast at a proposed **230°C conventional / 210°C fan**, turning as they colour. Start checking after about **30 minutes**. The wings and turkey frames should develop golden patches. Check thin wing tips and pieces of breast frame individually, moving browned pieces off the tray if others need longer. The actual turkey frame weight must be measured before scaling this example.

steps.title: Brown the aromatics
steps.text: Toss **300 g onion, 150 g carrot and 120 g celery with the remaining 15 ml oil**, add around the poultry parts and continue roasting until the parts are deeply golden-brown and the vegetables have browned edges. Check regularly, especially any thin pieces. Check after another **15 minutes** and keep turning and checking until evenly browned. Remove any blackened bits.

steps.title: Deglaze
steps.text: Transfer the browned **wings, turkey frames and vegetables** to the stockpot. Pour off excess fat from the roasting tray. Add a little **water**, scrape up the brown fond, and pour it into the stockpot. For the illustrative **3 kg combined-parts** batch, add any supplied **heart, cleaned gizzard and neck**, **3 thyme sprigs, 1½ bay leaves, 9 peppercorns** and optional **30 g tomato paste**. For the actual batch, use the scaled table amounts. Add more **water to just cover**. Record the total water added.

steps.title: Extract gently
steps.text: Bring to a simmer, skim surface foam, and maintain gentle bubbling. Begin assessing the stock after **2½ hours**, using **2½–3 hours** as the turkey-specific reference range. Top up with a little **water** only as needed to keep the bones covered. Taste for a rounded roasted poultry flavour with turkey character. The mixed stock’s flavour and body need assessing in this batch.

steps.title: Strain and defat
steps.text: Lift out large solids, then pass through a fine sieve into a clean pot without mashing the vegetables. Skim fat carefully or use a fat separator. Measure the strained stock. Reserve a small amount for sauce adjustment if useful, cooling and freezing it separately.

notes: Steps 1–3 repeat the **3 kg combined-parts example**. Before cooking, calculate every amount from the actual total weight using the table; the example does not assume these crowns provide 1 kg of frames.

**Pressure-cooker alternative.** If all the wings, turkey frames and liquid fit the Instant Pot within its model-specific fill limits, use the roasted ingredients in the cooker. **90 minutes at high pressure with natural release** is the brown-chicken reference process to adapt. Check the actual cooker instructions and poultry piece sizes.

method.heading: Take the stock close to demi before freezing

steps.title: Optional Madeira infusion
steps.text: For each **1 litre of unreduced stock allocated**, simmer **75 ml Madeira with 30 g sliced shallot** in a small pan until the wine volume is roughly one-third of its starting amount. Add this to the allocated **stock**. The shallot will be strained out.
steps.aside: This flavour option is our adaptation.

steps.title: Reduce and assess hot
steps.text: Simmer uncovered in the wide pan, skimming fat and foam. Check flavour and consistency increasingly often as it concentrates. Stop when the hot base tastes of roast poultry and lightly coats a spoon, keeping the **approximately 1 litre finished-sauce target** in view. If that balance is reached at a larger volume, keep the extra rather than reducing solely to reach 1 litre. Strain again and measure the volume. Reserve adjustment stock separately. If the pleasant coating is reached only below the needed volume, record the shortfall and plan extra stock; do not thin it to 1 litre regardless of flavour. The endpoint depends on the stock's strength and natural gelatine. A fixed reduction ratio cannot establish the yield.
steps.aside: This master’s default route freezes the base near serving concentration, with butter, vinegar and small consistency adjustments left for service.

steps.title: Cool and freeze
steps.text: Portion the hot base into shallow containers, cool quickly with an ice/cold-water bath and stirring, then refrigerate or freeze within **2 hours**. Keep chilled food at **4°C** and frozen food at **−18°C or below**. Label with contents, date, portion volume and whether Madeira has been added. Freeze the base and any reserved stock separately. Leave space for expansion. Use the freezer base within **3 months** under the project's Dutch leftover guidance.

notes: **Stock-first alternative.** At step 5, cool and freeze the strained stock with the same controls. After refrigerator thawing, carry out steps 6–7 on the day it will be served, then finish below. This moves more reduction work into the dinner weekend.

steps.title: Thaw in the fridge
steps.text: Move the portion needed to the fridge far enough ahead that it is fully thawed. About **24 hours** is a general guide for small portions, with longer possible for a deep container. Keep covered on a tray and check the centre. Plan to finish and serve on the same day after thawing.

steps.title: Reheat and adjust
steps.text: Put the thawed **base** into a saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring. Add a little thawed **reserved stock or water** if too concentrated, or reduce a little further if weak. Heat any added reserved stock through in the sauce. Assess while hot, aiming for a fluid, light coating.

steps.title: Finish off the heat
steps.text: For the **approximately 1 litre finished batch**, swirl **40 g cold butter** into the hot **sauce base**, then add **5 ml sherry vinegar**. Taste before adding any of the remaining **5 ml vinegar**, then adjust **salt**. If useful, add a little strained, defatted, fully cooked roulade juice and reassess. Measure the finished volume; use hot **reserved unsalted stock** as needed to adjust towards **1 litre**, provided the flavour and light coating remain right. Serve immediately, allowing **100–120 ml per turkey plate**. Scale butter/vinegar proportionately if finishing a different quantity.

items: Reheat only the portion required and serve after finishing. Food already reheated once is discarded if left over. Avoid thawing, reducing, chilling and then reheating again as the default service sequence. For the recommended route, extraction and reduction happen in one advance cooking session, followed by cooling/freezing and one final reheat.

If the stock reaches the desired flavour before it has enough body, stop reducing and assess the available cartilage-rich parts or a measured gelatine adjustment in the next revision. The **2 kg wing supplement** is now part of the banked base; further parts or powdered gelatine remain optional development choices. Do not force the reduction past a pleasant flavour to chase thickness. A cold gel shows natural gelatine is present, while the hot spoon test determines serving texture.

Weigh **1 kg potatoes**, keeping similar sizes together. Prepare **150 g cold butter**, with **50 g extra cold butter** separately available. Measure **125 ml milk**, with **60 ml extra milk** separately available. Warm the milk for incorporation; keep the butter cold.

If preparing ahead, have shallow cooling containers, lids and labels ready. For reheating, use the portion needed and set out a saucepan and a little extra milk, amount as needed and recorded separately.

steps.text: Cover **1 kg scrubbed whole potatoes** with cold water. Bring to a boil, then simmer until very soft, approximately **30–40 minutes**, depending on size.
Drain. Handle with a tea towel and peel while hot. Rice or mill all the **cooked potatoes**, then push through the fine sieve for the smoothest finish.
Return the **sieved potato** to low heat and stir for **1 minute** to release moisture.

Gradually incorporate **150 g cold butter** and **125 ml warm milk**, stirring by hand. If wanted, add up to **50 g more butter**; adjust with up to **60 ml more warm milk**. Add **salt to taste**. Record the amounts used. Serve promptly.

notes: Project texture cue: a glossy, soft mound that relaxes under the spoon, with room for demi beside it. This is a plating preference, not the source's almost-pourable endpoint. No blender or electric mixer.

items: Fresh service is the base method. Advance preparation remains a service option, not a confirmed commitment.

recipes.title: Beans, snow peas and sprouts
recipes.subtitle: Raw and charred, served at room temperature

batch: **Reference batch:** 1 kg trimmed raw vegetables plus dressing. **Dinner portions, finished yield and multiplier: TBD.** Eight guests are confirmed overall; this is not a measured ten-portion recipe.

items: Set out scales, board, sharp knife or mandoline, large blanching pan, ice-water bowl, slotted spoon, clean towels/spinner, wide heavy frying pan, tray, dressing bowl and tongs.

Prepare **400 g trimmed green beans**, **200 g trimmed snow peas** and **400 g trimmed sprouts**, divided into **200 g finely shredded raw sprouts + 200 g halved or quartered sprouts for blanching and charring**. Quarter larger sprouts so the centres cook evenly. Keep the raw shreds separate.

Measure **100 ml olive oil**, divided into **90 ml dressing + 10 ml charring**. Prepare **60 g finely diced shallot, 45 ml champagne vinegar, 30 g finely chopped pitted dates and 20 g finely grated Parmesan**. Set out **3 g fine salt**, divided into **2 g dressing + 1 g sprouts**, with black pepper.
Prepare **4 L blanching water with 40 g salt**, separate from the seasoning salt, and ice water as needed. Have clean covered containers ready if preparing components ahead.

rows.name: Parmesan

steps.title: Make the dressing
steps.text: Mix **60 g shallot, 45 ml champagne vinegar and 2 g salt**. Let the shallot lose its harsh raw edge. Stir in **30 g dates and 20 g grated Parmesan**, then whisk in **90 ml olive oil** and **black pepper to taste**. Taste with a piece of vegetable: aim for tangy, savoury dressing with small date accents.
steps.aside: The maceration duration remains TBD; this sensory cue is a working adaptation.

steps.title: Blanch the beans and snow peas separately
steps.text: Bring **4 L water with 40 g salt** to a boil. Cook **400 g beans** until crisp-tender, then transfer to **ice water**. Cook **200 g snow peas** until bright green and still crisp, then refresh separately. Drain and dry thoroughly. Leave the beans whole and halve the snow peas diagonally.
steps.aside: Cooking durations depend on the actual vegetables and remain TBD.

steps.title: Prepare the sprouts for charring
steps.text: Blanch only the **200 g halved/quartered sprouts** until just tender enough for a knife tip to enter the base, retaining bite. Refresh in **ice water**, drain and dry the cut faces thoroughly. Keep the **200 g raw shredded sprouts** uncooked.
steps.aside: The blanch-and-char sequence is an untested adaptation.

steps.title: Char
steps.text: Heat the wide pan over medium-high heat. Add **10 ml olive oil**, then the **200 g dried sprout halves/quarters**, cut faces down in one uncrowded layer. Let the faces colour before moving; turn as needed until deeply browned in places and tender through the centres. Season with **1 g salt**. Transfer to a shallow tray so steam escapes. Aim for toasted edges, not an all-over black coating.
steps.aside: Pan capacity and cooking duration are TBD; split the same 10 ml oil proportionally if batching.

steps.title: Bring together at room temperature
steps.text: For same-day service, let the freshly charred sprouts lose their heat before combining. If components were refrigerated, take out only the quantity needed near service and let them lose their refrigerator chill under the handling limits below. Do not mix hot sprouts into the raw shreds. There is no validated tempering time; room temperature is the chosen presentation, not a holding method.

steps.title: Dress and plate
steps.text: Combine the **400 g beans, 200 g snow peas and 200 g raw shredded sprouts**. Add the **prepared dressing** a little at a time, using only enough to coat without pooling. Gently fold in the **200 g charred sprouts**, keeping browned faces visible. Taste, adjust seasoning if needed and record any adjustment. Keep unused dressing back. Serve promptly at room temperature, away from pooled turkey demi.

items: Dressing and cooked vegetables can be prepared separately, cooled promptly and refrigerated in clean covered containers at **4°C**, within **2 hours** of cooking. Use within **2 days** and follow any shorter ingredient-pack limits. Wash and dry raw sprouts; shred on the service day as a proposed quality choice.
Prefer charring on the service day for browned flavour and texture; no crisp crust after storage or dressing is guaranteed. This is a quality preference, not an agreed task placement.

Bring out only the quantity needed for the room-temperature presentation, serve promptly, and keep total time outside refrigeration within **2 hours**, including cooling/tempering and service. No extended counter hold is approved.

Keep dressing separate until assembly. Any refrigerated leftovers retain the original preparation limit; bringing to room temperature does not reset it. If cooked components are reheated instead, heat until steaming throughout and reheat only once.

recipes.title: Roast Hokkaido pumpkin
recipes.subtitle: Cardamom-nigella onion, seeds, yogurt, chervil
batch: **Batch:** 1.25 kg deseeded Hokkaido pumpkin, skin on, with toppings below. This is the 1 kg reference batch × 1.25, with rounded spoon and weight amounts. **Finished yield and per-plate weight: TBD.** Eight guests are confirmed overall. Roasting shrinks the pumpkin, so the planning yardstick is about 100 g cooked pumpkin per head plus onion and toppings; neither that yardstick nor the 1.25× margin is a measured yield. The earlier draft's ten small portions were an allowance, not a measured yield.

items: Set out a sturdy board, strong knife, scales, measuring tools, two lined rimmed roasting trays, wide frying pan, small dry pan, spatula, tongs and clean serving spoons. Confirm usable tray space.

Wash and deseed the Hokkaido; weigh **1.25 kg prepared pumpkin**, skin on, and cut into wedges approximately **4 cm wide at the outer edge**. Slice **210 g peeled red onion** thinly. Weigh **25 g butter, 40 g pumpkin seeds and 190 g Greek yogurt**. Pick **4 g chervil leaves and tender tips**, keeping them separate from the cooking ingredients.

Measure **60 ml olive oil**, divided into **40 ml roasting + 20 ml onions**; **1 tsp salt**, divided into **⅝ tsp roasting + ⅜ tsp onions**; and **1⅝ tsp nigella seeds**, divided into **1¼ tsp onions + ⅜ tsp finish**. Set out **1 tbsp + 1 tsp caster sugar, ⅝ tsp ground cumin, ⅝ tsp ground coriander, ⅜ tsp ground turmeric, 5 lightly crushed cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 green chilli halved lengthways and 60 ml vegetable stock**.
Keep the **190 g yogurt and 4 g chervil** refrigerated while the hot components cook, following their pack instructions. Reserve both for finishing.

steps.title: Roast the pumpkin
steps.text: Heat the oven to **220°C conventional / 200°C fan**, the existing draft's working setting. Toss **1.25 kg Hokkaido wedges with 40 ml olive oil, 1 tbsp + 1 tsp caster sugar and ⅝ tsp salt**. Arrange with a broad cut face against the parchment, leaving gaps; use both trays if needed. Roast until cut faces are browned and a knife enters the flesh easily while wedges retain their shape. Turn to colour the other cut face as needed.
steps.aside: Exact duration for these wedges is **TBD**; the earlier untested 30–40-minute estimate is not a verified cooking time.

steps.title: Soften the onion
steps.text: Heat **25 g butter and 20 ml olive oil** over medium heat. Add **210 g red onion** and cook, stirring, until soft with lightly golden edges, without taking it to a dark caramel.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Stir in **⅝ tsp cumin, ⅝ tsp ground coriander, ⅜ tsp turmeric, 1¼ tsp nigella seeds, 5 lightly crushed cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick and 1 halved green chilli**. Cook gently until aromatic, without scorching the ground spices. Add **60 ml vegetable stock and ⅜ tsp salt**; simmer until the onion is tender and the liquid has nearly evaporated. Remove the **cardamom pods, cinnamon stick and chilli**.
steps.aside: This low-liquid onion treatment is an untested adaptation.

steps.title: Toast the seeds
steps.text: Toast **40 g pumpkin seeds** in a dry pan, moving them until fragrant and lightly coloured. Tip onto a plate to stop cooking. Keep separate until finishing.

steps.title: Combine and assess
steps.text: Spoon the cooked **spiced red onion** around and between the **roasted pumpkin wedges**, turning gently only where needed. Avoid breaking the wedges or coating every browned face. Taste a piece with a little of the reserved **190 g yogurt**; adjust salt only if needed and record additions. Keep any unused tasting yogurt separate from the serving batch using clean utensils.

steps.title: Plate and finish
steps.text: Plate the warm **pumpkin and onion** with small spoonfuls from the **190 g yogurt** beside the wedges. Distribute the **40 g toasted pumpkin seeds** and reserved **⅜ tsp nigella**. Finish with **4 g fresh chervil leaves and tender tips** immediately before serving, after all cooking/reheating. Leave small leaves whole.
steps.aside: Actual per-plate quantities remain TBD; measure any unused topping rather than forcing it onto the plates.

items: Proposed quality preference: cook the onion separately ahead; roast the pumpkin on the service day if oven capacity permits. This is not an agreed task schedule. Chilling and reheating can soften the browned edges; performance is untested.
Cool cooked pumpkin and onion promptly in separate shallow containers; refrigerate within **2 hours**, covered at **4°C**, and use within **2 days**. Follow any shorter ingredient instructions.

If reheating, heat only the amount needed until steaming throughout, handling wedges gently. Reheat once only and discard reheated leftovers. Reheating temperature/duration and oven overlap remain TBD; no crispy-edge guarantee is made.

Keep **yogurt and chervil** separate and refrigerated until finishing; follow pack instructions. Add toasted seeds and chervil only after reheating. No freezing or prolonged warm-holding route is specified.

recipes.title: Vanilla cheesecake
recipes.subtitle: Gluten-free digestive base
batch: **Texture goal:** creamy and softly set, holding a clean slice without a firm, dense interior. Retain the filling amounts below; do not add flour/starch or extra eggs to make slicing easier.

**Batch:** one full-size cake in the **confirmed 23 cm springform tin**. Use Sally’s original **1× filling**. Her published yield is **12–16 slices**; actual adapted yield/portion weight is unmeasured. Eight guests are confirmed; Daniela now welcomes extra plain cheesecake, superseding the smaller ten-slice cake. Cut elegant slices as needed rather than dividing the whole cake into eight large portions. Compote and shards remain allocated for **10 garnished servings**; extra cake can be kept plain.

items: Use a conventional oven at **177°C** (350°F; fan adjustment unverified), lower-middle shelf, a 23 cm springform, roasting tin large enough to surround it, heavy-duty foil, rack, mixer/paddle, scales and kettle. Check water-bath/tin fit before mixing.

Set out the filling ingredients below at room temperature for smooth mixing. Use **904 g Philadelphia cream cheese**, the confirmed brand. Choose plain **Original**, not Light or whipped, as the working full-fat product recommendation. US block cheese is Sally’s tested format; her non-US note allows that local tub cheese may work, but reports reader experience rather than her own testing. Check the actual pack variant and label; do not alter the filling merely because it comes in a Dutch tub.

Grind **200 g gluten-free digestives** finely. Have **85 g melted unsalted butter**, **67 g base sugar** and a flat-bottomed cup ready. Use GF-labelled biscuits; taste them first for chalkiness. Keep ordinary biscuit crumbs away from this station.
At the pass: chilled cake, chilled compote, dry pistachio shards, **1 washed orange**, zester, sharp knife, warm water for the knife, clean cloth and eight plates.
